title: Ankle/Foot Active Range of Motion
purpose: Basic active range of motion (AROM) assessment of the ankle-foot complex.
structure: Talocrural joint (dorsiflexion/plantarflexion), subtalar (talocalcaneal) joint (inversion/eversion) and the toes (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction).
procedure: Patient supine with legs fully extended and feet hanging off the edge of the table. Dorsiflexion: bring the feet as far as possible towards the body; plantarflexion: as far away as possible. Inversion: bring the soles together; eversion: bring the soles apart. Toe flexion: curl the toes; toe extension: pull the toes up; toe abduction: spread the toes; toe adduction: bring the toes together (the last two may be difficult for some patients).
positive: Not a pass/fail test: compare range and quality of movement with the other side.

accuracy.source: n/a (basic assessment; page lists no references)

notes: Basic assessment page, not a diagnostic test. The page uses the European convention: eversion = combined dorsiflexion + abduction + pronation; inversion = combined plantarflexion + supination + adduction. Companion pages: passive ROM and resisted isometric testing of the ankle/foot.

title: Ankle/Foot Passive Range of Motion
purpose: Basic passive range of motion (PROM) assessment of the ankle-foot complex: osteokinematic range in degrees and end-feel when limited.
structure: Talocrural joint (plantarflexion, dorsiflexion) and subtalar joint (inversion, eversion).
procedure: Plantarflexion: patient supine close to the long edge of the bench, knee flexed to 90 degrees; one hand around the talus (web space or hypothenar), the other hand grasps the plantar aspect of the calcaneus; move the foot into plantarflexion and assess end-feel. Dorsiflexion: same position; one hand fixates tibia and fibula, the other hand on the plantar aspect of the foot as close to the talus as possible; move into dorsiflexion and assess end-feel. Inversion (plantarflexion + adduction + supination) and eversion (dorsiflexion + abduction + pronation) at the subtalar joint are shown in a separate linked video.
positive: Not a pass/fail test: range in degrees and end-feel compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: n/a (basic assessment). Reliability: Alawna et al. 2019 found excellent inter- and intra-rater reliability for goniometer and smartphone inclinometer measurement of ankle ROM

notes: Basic assessment page. References also list normative ROM data (Soucie et al. 2011; McKay et al. 2017, 1000 Norms Project). The page mentions an end-feel table that is not reproduced in the text.

title: Ankle/Foot Resisted Isometric Testing
purpose: Basic resisted isometric strength assessment of the ankle-foot complex.
structure: Ankle dorsiflexors and plantarflexors (talocrural joint), invertors and evertors (subtalar/talocalcaneonavicular joint), toe extensors and flexors; the page also includes knee flexion.
procedure: Knee flexion: patient supine, knee flexed to about 30 degrees, resistance above the ankle, patient pulls the heel towards the buttock. Dorsiflexion: knee flexed 90 degrees, fixate, apply downward pressure on the dorsum of the foot while the patient resists. Plantarflexion: resistance at the sole. Inversion: fixate the tibia, hold the foot, patient turns the sole inwards against resistance. Eversion: fixate the tibia dorsally, patient turns the sole outwards against resistance. Big-toe extension and toe flexion: fixate the foot, hold the big toe, patient pulls the toe up or curls it against resistance.
positive: Not a pass/fail test: compare strength and pain response with the other side.

accuracy.source: n/a (basic assessment; page lists no references)

notes: Basic assessment page, not a diagnostic test. ⚠ The page lists knee flexion as the first movement of the ankle/foot isometric screen; this is as written on the source page. Companion pages: active and passive ROM of the ankle/foot.

title: Weight Bearing Lunge Test
purpose: Continuous (quantitative) measure of weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion range of motion.
procedure: Wall-distance technique with a tape measure: the patient faces a wall and lunges towards it, trying to touch the wall with the knee while keeping the foot flat on the floor (heel down). Measure the distance from the wall to the big toe. Move the foot back as long as the knee can still touch the wall with the foot planted; the largest distance is the score. Variants in the literature measure the front or back limb with an inclinometer or tape measure; Powden et al. 2015 found no significant reliability differences between techniques.
positive: A wall distance of at least 5 inches / 12.5 cm is considered normal (rule of thumb: one hand width). A change of 1.9 cm is needed to exceed measurement error when tracking progress. An anterior pinching sensation suggests a joint (arthrogenic) restriction; a calf stretch sensation suggests soft-tissue restriction.

accuracy.source: n/a (ROM measure, not a diagnostic test). Reliability and minimal detectable change: Powden et al. 2015 systematic review (Man Ther)

notes: Limited ankle dorsiflexion is described as a contributing factor in patellofemoral pain and in foot over-pronation possibly leading to plantar fasciitis. Source writes the cut-off as '12,5 cm' (comma decimal).

title: Anterior Drawer Test Ankle
purpose: Detect anterior talocrural joint laxity (anterior talofibular ligament insufficiency) after ankle inversion trauma.
structure: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and talocrural joint capsule.
procedure: Patient supine, thigh supported on the table, knee flexed, ankle held in 10-15 degrees of plantarflexion. Grasp the heel with the patient's foot resting on the anterior aspect of your forearm; with the other hand hold back the tibia and draw the foot anteriorly.
positive: Increased anterior translation compared with the unaffected ankle; a dimple ('suction sign') may appear over the anterolateral talus. Croy et al. 2013 used ultrasound cut-offs of 2.3 mm and 3.7 mm talofibular interval.

accuracy.source: Croy et al. 2013 (JOSPT), ultrasound reference standard

notes: Source rates the test as weak clinical value overall; accuracy rises with larger talofibular interval. Miller et al. 2016 (cadaver study) found that letting the talocrural joint internally rotate around the intact deltoid ligament (anterolateral drawer) detects more subtle instability. Companion test: talar tilt test. Source writes the cut-offs as '2,3mm' and '3,7mm' (comma decimals).

title: Talar Tilt Test
purpose: Assess the lateral ankle ligaments (and, in one step, the medial deltoid complex) after inversion trauma.
structure: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), calcaneofibular ligament (CFL), posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL); deltoid ligament complex on eversion.
procedure: Patient sitting with the knee hanging off the table. ATFL: foot in plantarflexion so the ligament is perpendicular to the movement, grasp the calcaneus and invert. CFL: foot in anatomical (neutral) position, invert and evert; the eversion component stresses the deltoid complex. PTFL: foot in maximal dorsiflexion, repeat the inversion.
positive: Pain, or excessive gapping compared with the unaffected side, in any of the positions.

accuracy.sensitivity: 50% (Hertel 1999, lateral ankle sprain); 4% (Rosen 2015, instability by gapping)
accuracy.source: Hertel et al. 1999 (Med Sci Sports Exerc); Rosen et al. 2015 (Scand J Med Sci Sports)

notes: Source rates the clinical value as moderate. Companion test: anterior drawer test of the ankle.

title: Anterior Ankle Impingement Diagnosis
purpose: History and examination cluster for non-invasive diagnosis of anterolateral ankle impingement.
structure: Anterolateral gutter of the ankle: synovial hypertrophy, cartilage proliferation, scar tissue, calcification or osteophytes after dorsiflexion trauma, inversion trauma or repetitive stress.
procedure: Check six findings (Liu et al. 1997): (1) anterolateral ankle joint tenderness; (2) anterolateral swelling (probably synovitis); (3) pain with forced dorsiflexion and eversion (narrows the anterolateral gutter); (4) pain with single-leg squat on the affected side; (5) pain with activities requiring dorsiflexion (stairs down, squatting, sport); (6) absence of ankle instability (check with the anterior drawer test).

accuracy.source: Liu et al. 1997 (Am J Sports Med), retrospective analysis of 22 cases vs MRI

notes: Source gives only moderate clinical value because of the wide confidence intervals and retrospective design (n=22). Companion tests: forced dorsiflexion sign (anterior impingement), heel thrust test (posterior impingement).

title: Forced Dorsiflexion Sign
purpose: Provocation test for anterior (anterolateral) ankle impingement.
structure: Hypertrophic synovium / osteophytes in the anterolateral gutter impinging between talus and lateral malleolus.
procedure: Patient sitting. Grasp the calcaneus with one hand and press the thumb of that hand over the anterolateral ankle (this may already be uncomfortable but is not yet positive). With the other hand move the foot into maximal dorsiflexion while maintaining thumb pressure.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's pain, or an increase of the pain elicited by the thumb pressure.

accuracy.source: Molloy et al. 2003 (J Bone Joint Surg Br)

notes: Source rates the test as moderate clinical value because the single study is at risk of bias. ⚠ The page embeds the same YouTube video (IbRCCIDa5-8) as the heel thrust test page; one video covers both signs. Source writes the sensitivity as '94,8%' (comma decimal).

title: Heel Thrust Test
purpose: Provocation test for posterior ankle impingement.
structure: Posterior ankle structures (posterior impingement after plantarflexion-dominant inversion trauma).
procedure: Patient supine with the ankle hanging over the edge of the bench and the foot relaxed. Place the base of the palm over the heel with one hand, stabilise the tibia with the other hand, and apply a horizontal thrust to the heel.

accuracy.source: none; page states no reliability or validity studies exist (test first described by Laslett 1988)

notes: Clinical value unknown according to the source. ⚠ The page's reference section is empty ('-') although the text cites Laslett (1988). ⚠ The embedded video (IbRCCIDa5-8) is the same as on the forced dorsiflexion sign page. Posterior pain typically persists while the anterolateral pain of a sprain subsides.

title: Cuboid Syndrome
purpose: Recognise cuboid syndrome as a cause of persistent lateral ankle/foot pain after inversion sprain, and perform the repositioning manipulation described in the literature.
structure: Calcaneocuboid joint; cuboid left in a relatively supinated position after torsion against navicular, cuneiform and calcaneus during a severe inversion trauma.
procedure: Diagnosis is a hypothesis built on history, cluster of signs, differential diagnosis and mechanism: pain localised over the calcaneocuboid joint while lateral ligament tenderness subsides, antalgic gait with more pain at push-off, absent joint play if testable. Manipulation (into relative pronation): patient supine, leg extended, foot over the edge of the bench; stand medial to the foot; hypothenar of the contralateral hand on the lateral-plantar cuboid just proximal to the base of the 5th metatarsal, hypothenar of the other hand dorsomedially on the cuboid (lateral and proximal to the line between 3rd and 4th toes); forearms in a straight line, hands folded; patient actively dorsiflexes maximally to pre-tension the cuboid in submaximal eversion; build compression through the elbows and pronation pre-tension; patient relaxes, then deliver a pronation swing with both elbows combined with a compression impulse of both hypothenars.
positive: Not a diagnostic test; the case series reports patients pain-free the following day after manipulation.

accuracy.source: n/a; Jennings & Davies 2005 (JOSPT) case series on treatment

notes: Up to 40% of ankle sprains leave residual symptoms; the cuboid hypothesis is offered for persistent lateral pain and is reported to be more prevalent in professional ballet dancers. ⚠ Filed by the source under 'Ankle & Foot Assessment' but the page and video mainly show a treatment technique; the only reference is a case series. Source advises excluding fracture first (Ottawa ankle rules).

title: Syndesmosis Injury Signs & Symptoms
purpose: History items that raise or lower suspicion of a distal tibiofibular syndesmosis injury after ankle trauma.
procedure: Ask first the sensitive items: inability to walk after injury; inability to hop. If positive, together with sensitive tests (syndesmosis ligament tenderness, dorsiflexion-external rotation stress test), ask the more specific items: pain out of proportion for a usual inversion sprain; pain felt in the shank or knee at the time of injury. Also note the mechanism (maximal dorsiflexion + external rotation with the foot planted) and perform the squeeze test as a specific confirmatory test.
positive: Each item is interpreted by its own sensitivity/specificity (see accuracy).

accuracy.sensitivity: inability to walk 89%; inability to hop 89%; pain out of proportion 65%; pain in shank/knee at injury 50%
accuracy.specificity: inability to walk 21%; inability to hop 29%; pain out of proportion 79%; pain in shank/knee at injury 70%
accuracy.source: Sman et al. 2015 as cited in text; reference list gives Sman et al. 2013 systematic review (Br J Sports Med)

notes: Return to sport is more than 4 times longer when the syndesmosis is involved (text: 15 days average for usual inversion trauma, Sman 2014). Swelling is often minimal so patients load too early; pain is usually located higher than in a plain inversion sprain. ⚠ Text cites Sman et al. (2015) for the numbers but the reference list only gives Sman et al. (2013). Source writes '600.000 people' and '3,5%' (European number formatting).

title: Syndesmosis Ligament Tenderness
purpose: Palpation screen for syndesmosis injury after ankle trauma.
structure: Anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL), interosseous ligament and membrane, transverse ligament, posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL).
procedure: Palpate the AITFL between talus and fibula, then continue proximally over the interosseous ligament and membrane. Then palpate the transverse ligament posteriorly and inferiorly between tibia and fibula, and slightly more proximally the posterior tibiofibular ligament.
positive: Tenderness or pain on any of the four structures. Tenderness over the interosseous membrane is associated with a more severe injury and longer recovery.

accuracy.source: Sman et al. 2015 (Br J Sports Med)

notes: Source: moderate value to exclude a syndesmosis injury, not helpful to confirm it. ⚠ This page states (Hunt 2013) that almost 25% of ankle sprains involve the syndesmosis, whereas the Cotton, fibular translation and squeeze pages quote the Dutch KNGF guideline at about 1%; the dorsiflexion-external rotation page gives a 1-24% range.

title: Dorsiflexion External Rotation Stress Test
purpose: Reproduce the mechanism of injury to stress the ankle syndesmosis (also called Kleiger's test).
structure: Interosseous membrane and ligament, AITFL, PITFL, transverse ligament.
procedure: Patient sitting with the knee hanging off the table at 90 degrees. Bring the talocrural joint into maximal dorsiflexion and apply an external rotation stress to the foot and ankle.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's anterolateral pain over the syndesmosis.

accuracy.source: Sman et al. 2013 as cited on the page (Br J Sports Med systematic review)

notes: Source rates stand-alone use as rather weak. The external rotation test as used by Beumer et al. 2002 was performed without dorsiflexion and showed very low accuracy; dorsiflexion widens the mortise and is considered integral to the test. Incidence of syndesmosis injury among ankle sprains quoted as 1-24%.

title: Syndesmosis Squeeze Test
purpose: Provocation test for syndesmosis injury by compressing tibia and fibula.
procedure: Patient supine. Compress tibia and fibula together from the lateral side ('squeeze'), starting proximally and moving slowly distally until the malleoli are reached.
positive: Pain during the squeeze, provided fracture, contusion and compartment syndrome have been ruled out. According to Nussbaum et al. 2001 the more proximal the pain is provoked, the more severe the injury.

accuracy.source: Sman et al. 2015 (Br J Sports Med)

notes: Source: rather weak accuracy to confirm a syndesmosis lesion. Quotes the Dutch KNGF guideline: syndesmosis injury is about 1% of all ankle injuries. Reference list also includes de César et al. 2011 and Sman et al. 2013.

title: Fibular Translation Test
purpose: Assess syndesmosis injury by translating the fibula on the tibia.
procedure: Patient side-lying; stand at the side of the patient's heel. Fixate the tibia with one hand and translate the fibula anteriorly and posteriorly with the other hand.
positive: Pain during the translations, or more movement on the affected side than on the unaffected side.

accuracy.source: Beumer et al. (text says 2011; reference list gives Beumer et al. 2002, Acta Orthop Scand)

notes: ⚠ Year mismatch on the source page: text cites Beumer et al. (2011), the only reference listed is Beumer et al. (2002). Quotes the Dutch KNGF guideline: syndesmosis injury about 1% of ankle injuries.

title: Cotton Test
purpose: Test for syndesmosis instability (separation of tibia and fibula).
structure: Distal tibiofibular syndesmosis (four ligaments holding tibia and fibula together).
procedure: Stabilise the distal tibia and fibula with one hand and apply a lateral translation force to the foot with the other hand.
positive: Translation of more than 3-5 mm, or a clunk heard or felt.
notes: Only sensitivity was measured (25%). Quotes the Dutch KNGF guideline: syndesmosis injury about 1% of all ankle injuries.

title: Crossed Leg Test
purpose: Provocation test for syndesmotic (high) ankle sprain.
structure: Distal tibiofibular syndesmosis; mechanism assumed similar to the squeeze test.
procedure: Patient seated, crosses the affected leg over the contralateral knee so the pivot point is around the middle or distal third of the lower leg. The patient then pushes down on the knee of the crossed leg. Pushing is unnecessary if pain already appears just from crossing the leg.

accuracy.source: Grosterlinden et al. 2016 (Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc), single study; also Netterstrom-Wedin & Bleakley 2021 meta-analysis listed

notes: Only one study has examined accuracy; the source calls the test of questionable utility. Mechanism of injury (Hunt 2015): forced external rotation of the dorsiflexed foot.
